power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: What we see depends on context.
From low to high levels of the visual system hierarchy, the amplitude of contextual influences is a func on of local input strength.
In the case of human face percep on, the influence exerted by face context on local feature discrimina on is determined by that feature discriminability.
Face contextual modula ons are presumed to rely on high-level, specialized contextual mechanisms, with li le contribu on of low-level mechanisms.
The shared dependence of low-and high-level contextual modula ons on local input strength however suggests they may be linked func onally.

The present registered report addresses this gap by inves ga ng whether consistent individual differences exist in contextual modula ons across low-level contrast detec on and high-level facial feature discrimina on.
Across tasks, we manipulated the contrast (i.e., strength) of a local input target (local gra ng and eye region, respec vely) presented either in isola on or embedded in context.
The context in the contrast detec on task refers to a larger surrounding gra ng while it refers to the facial features surrounding the target eye region in the facial feature discrimina on task.
The comparison of contrast thresholds across condi ons provided a metric to evaluate contextual modula on magnitudes.

For both upright feature discrimina on and contrast detec on, context exerted a strong suppressive influence on local target processing; i.e., incongruent face context and parallel surround increased contrast threshold for feature discrimina on and gra ng detec on, respec vely, compared to isolated viewing condi on.
As expected, face inversion dras cally reduced the influence of context on local contrast threshold.

We found no conclusive proof of a func onal link between the magnitude of contextual modula on in local contrast detec on and face feature matching; there was however extreme evidence for the correla on of contextual modula on magnitude in upright and inverted face feature matching.

By inves ga ng the shared variance between the contextual modula on magnitudes across visual processing levels, this study aimed at a system-wide understanding of the influence of spa al context on vision.
Despite low-and high-level contextual modula ons sharing similar opera ng principles, the present findings suggest they may involve independent mechanisms.
We outline methodological approaches for further research development on this topic.

text.text: The processing of the human face, among other visual categories, is par cularly suscep ble to contextual modula ons.

Facial features are more accurately discriminated or recognized when they are part of a complete face (context) compared to when they are presented in isola on or in an atypical context, such as a scrambled face (Bruce, 1988; Davidoff & Donnelly, 1990; Sergent, 1984; Tanaka & Farah, 1993), resul ng in the so-called whole-part advantage.

text.text: Another manifesta on of face contextual modula ons is observed with the composite face and congruency paradigms.

In these paradigms, the observer's sensi vity to a local feature decreases if it is incongruent with the surrounding context, in terms of either similarity status (when performing a discrimina on task) or iden ty (when performing a recogni on task; Anaki, Nica, & Moscovitch, 2011; Farah et al., 1998; Goffaux, 2009 Goffaux, , 2012;; Hole, 1994; Richler & Gauthier, 2014).

text.text: The vulnerability of face contextual modula ons to inversion has therefore been taken to suggest that the face contextual mechanisms are implemented at high-level stages of visual processing specifically tuned to the natural sta s cs of the human face (i.e., the regulari es in the way faces appear to us in everyday life, i.e., upright; e.g., Andrews et al., 2010; Goffaux et al., 2013; Liu-Shuang et al., 2015; Mazard, Schiltz, & Rossion, 2006; Schiltz et al., 2010; Schiltz & Rossion, 2006).

text.text: However, empirical evidence challenges a purely high-level account for face contextual modula ons.

First, the strength of contextual modula ons for faces depends on image proper es processed at primary stages of visual processing, such as spa al frequency (Boutet, Collin, & Faubert, 2003; Goffaux, 2009; Goffaux & Rossion, 2006) and orienta on (Dakin & Wa , 2009; Goffaux & Dakin, 2010).

text.text: Moreover, face contextual modula ons share similari es with low-level mechanisms in their dependence on local input strength.

Specifically, evidence indicates that the impact of the (face) context in a local feature discrimina on task is inversely related to the physical difference of the features at stake (Canoluk, Moors, & Goffaux, 2023; Goffaux, 2012; Goffaux et al., 2013).

text.text: This inverse rela onship between contextual influence and local input strength is shared with low-level contextual mechanisms.

For example, neurons in the primate visual cortex are more likely to integrate informa on across the visual field when the contrast of the local input is weak (Angelucci et al., 2017; Alessandra Angelucci et al., 2002; Levi & Lund, 1997).

text.text: Face contextual modula ons' reliance on low-level proper es, as well as the shared dependence on local input strength raises the rarely asked ques on of whether the inter-individual variability in face contextual mechanisms can be explained by low-level contextual mechanisms to some extent.

In a recent study, we aimed to answer this ques on by measuring the amount of shared variance in the magnitude of contextual modula ons for low-level contrast detec on and morphed facial feature discrimina on (in upright and inverted faces) by exploi ng their shared dependence on local input strength (Canoluk, Moors, & Goffaux, 2023).

text.text: We obtained contrast detec on thresholds for the lowlevel task and point of subjec ve equality (PSE) for the discrimina on of two subsequently displayed, morphed facial features (eyes) in matched contextual condi ons using a single Bayesian Hierarchical Model.
We found no evidence for the covariance of the contextual modula on magnitude in upright facial feature discrimina on and contrast detec on, which indicates they are governed by separate mechanisms.

On the other hand, there was substan al evidence that contextual modula on magnitude weakly covaried between contrast detec on and inverted facial feature discrimina on, sugges ng a rela onship between low-level and high-level, non-face-specialized contextual modula ons.

Lastly, there was decisive evidence for a strong correla on between upright and inverted face contextual modula ons which can be explained by the overlap in non-specialized mechanisms that these two kinds of s muli recruit, especially when the depicted iden es are unfamiliar to the par cipant (Burton, 2013; Megreya & Burton, 2006).

text.text: This difference in the local input proper es of the two tasks may have reduced the dependence of the contextual mechanisms recruited by facial feature discrimina on and contrast detec on.

Past findings indeed showed that contextual illusions employing a similar local input property (e.g., two different size illusions) are more likely to correlate (Grzeczkowski et al., 2017; see also Haberman, Brady, & Alvarez, 2015 for a similar comparison for ensemble percep on).

text.text: Furthermore, in the facial feature discrimina on task, the target (eye region) was displayed foveally, at ~1.3° eccentricity whereas the targets appeared at 5° of eccentricity in the contrast detec on task.
Past evidence indicates that contextual influences across fovea and periphery rely on non-overlapping mechanisms (Xing & Heeger, 2000).

text.text: Therefore, we reasoned that the differences in the employed local input property and foveal posi on of the targets could be the reason that we could not observe a dependence between contrast detec on and facial feature discrimina on tasks.

In this study, we aim to re-address the existence of a func onal link between low-and high-level contextual mechanisms by circumven ng possible interferences caused by these differences across tasks in the previous study.
First, we manipulated contrast at the eye region for the facial feature discrimina on task.
By doing so, the low-and high-level tasks involved the same local input property.

By measuring the magnitude of face contextual modula ons at varying degrees of contrast, we inves gated whether contextual modula ons exhibit a dependence on local contrast during face processing like they do in basic visual tasks.
Moreover, in the contrast detec on task, the targets were displayed closer to fovea, aiming to tap into the foveal contextual mechanisms as in the facial feature discrimina on task.
The comparison of the discrimina on/detec on contrast thresholds across different context condi ons provided a metric of contextual modula on magnitude.

A correla on of contextual modula on magnitudes between upright facial feature discrimina on and contrast detec on would demonstrate that the inter-subject variability in face contextual modula ons is to some extent explained by low-level contextual mechanisms (H1).
An absence of correla on would bring further support to the specializa on and independence of face contextual mechanisms.

Second, we inves gated the correla on between inverted facial feature discrimina on and contrast detec on to see how the par al disrup on of the face-specialized mechanisms caused by inversion influences the amount of shared variance with low-level mechanisms (H2).

Finally, we inves gated the correla on between upright facial feature discrimina on and inverted facial feature discrimina on contextual modula ons in order to quan fy the func onal overlap of the contextual mechanisms involved for these two s mulus types (H3).

text.text: For data collec on, we decided to opt for a sequen al design with a maximal sample size, which entails that data be gathered un l enough evidence has been accumulated or the predefined maximum number of par cipants has been tested.

text.text: In the facial feature discrimina on task, we presented pairs of whole faces or isolated eye regions.

The original s mulus set consisted of 32 full-frontal grayscale pictures (on a scale from 0 to 1; 600 x 700 pixels) of unfamiliar white neutral faces from each gender without glasses, facial hair, or makeup.
Face models were young adult students and alumni (aged 18-25 years) of the UCLouvain (Belgium), who gave wri en consent for the use of their image (Laguesse et al., 2012).

text.text: The luminance and root-mean-square (RMS) contrast of all face images were set to a mean of .52 and .12, respec vely (using MatLab, Na ck, MA).
Next, we ensured that the eye regions of faces were comparable in terms of inter-pupillary distance and physical similarity.
We measured inter-pupillary distance in each face image and paired the faces with comparable values (average pixel difference of 1.32 ± 1.31 pixels).
A er this ini al pairing, pixelwise similarity within the eye region was calculated within each pair using corr2 func on in MatLab.
The pixelwise similarity of the target eye region was .8 on average (SD = .014).
For each gender, the eight pairs lying within two standard devia ons around the mean pixelwise similarity distribu on were paired; the remaining eight pairs were only used as "face contexts".
An addi onal set of 12 female faces (six pairs of female faces) which had undergone the same procedure were selected for prac ce trials.

We extracted the target region (eyes and brows) of each selected pair using a single aperture within the same pair (so the subjects could not rely on the shape of the aperture between two images within a pair) and blended it onto two "face contexts" whose eye areas were a priori replaced with a smooth skin texture (using Adobe Photoshop CS., Berkeley, CA), therefore all presented s muli were edited, to ensure similarity across experimental trials.
Each face subtended a visual angle of ~7° in height, and ~5.2° in width.

text.text: For inverted faces, contextual modula ons were also present (Outcome-Neutral Test 2), but their overall magnitude was smaller than for upright faces.

Both contextual condi ons showed credibly higher thresholds than the isolated condi on (context-vs. isolated: median = 2.12, 95% HDI [1.85,2.38]; context+ vs. isolated: median = 1.56, 95% HDI [1.30,1.82], with both HDI en rely outside the ROPE).
To assess whether upright faces are processed more contextually than inverted faces (Outcome Neutral Test 3), we compared the magnitude of the contextual effects across the two tasks.

Using a ROPE of ±0.18, the contextual effect was credibly larger for upright faces (median = 3.04, 95% HDI [2.66,3.42]) than for inverted faces (median = 0.56, 95% HDI [0.22,0.87]), as indicated by the posterior distribu on of the difference between these two effects (median difference = 2.48, 95% HDI [2.00,2.95], HDI laying en rely outside the ROPE).
These results confirm that contextual processing is substan ally more pronounced for upright faces.

The residual values obtained from this procedure were then used to compute correla ons across tasks (see Methods).
These magnitude correla ons provided a quan ta ve assessment of the rela onship between contextual modula ons across tasks (see Figure 5).

The correla on between contrast detec on and inverted face discrimina on was numerically larger but eviden ally weak, with only anecdotal evidence for the null (r = .19, BF₀₁ = 1.51, BF₁₀ = .66).

text.text: Modula on by context is a fundamental computa onal principle of visual processing (Mareschal, Sceniak, & Shapley, 2001; Nurminen & Angelucci, 2014) thought to reduce spa al redundancies of sensory input and enable sparse, efficient and feature-selec ve neural code at all levels of the visual system's hierarchy (Angelucci et al., 2017; Field, 1987; Vinje & Gallant, 2002).

text.text: A first step in this direc on is to inves gate the func onal rela onship of contextual modula ons across visual processing levels.

To do so, we compared contextual modula ons at lowand high-level stages of processing in the same group of par cipants using a comparable metric, namely the level of contrast necessary to reach threshold performance to detect or discriminate local targets presented either in isola on or in context.

We reasoned that using a similar metric would op mize the chance to observe a func onal link between low-and high-level contextual modula ons (see Canoluk, Moors, & Goffaux, 2023 for a similar approach).

text.text: In the low-level task (adapted from Canoluk, Moors, & Goffaux, 2023; Mannion, Donkin, & Whi ord, 2017), par cipants detected a gra ng presented in either a parallel (context-), an orthogonal context (context+), or isola on.

text.text: In the highlevel tasks, par cipants matched pairs of upright or inverted eye regions presented either in isola on, congruent (context+) or in incongruent (context-) upright or inverted face contexts.
In both tasks, local target contrast was adap vely stair-cased.
In the low-level task, the local gra ng was less well detected when embedded in a parallel context than when presented in an orthogonal context or in isola on.
There was no conclusive evidence for the influence of the orthogonal context on contrast detec on.
These findings are in line with past evidence of a mainly suppressive influence of parallel surround on gra ng detec on (Canoluk, Moors, & Goffaux, 2023; Mannion, Donkin, & Whi ord, 2017).

text.text: In upright faces, incongruent context increased local contrast thresholds for facial feature discrimina on compared to congruent and isolated condi on.

While it is standard prac ce to quan fy low-level contextual modula ons in terms of contrast threshold, we have no knowledge of past use of this metric to quan fy contextual modula ons in face percep on.
Whether congruent context facilitated facial feature discrimina on rela ve to the isolated condi on was inconclusive.

The mainly suppressive influence of (incongruent) face context on local feature percep on has been extensively documented in past studies (Goffaux, 2012; Rossion, 2013; Suzuki & Cavanagh, 1998; Young, Hellawell, & Hay, 1987), which showed that incongruent context shi s the level of shape dissimilarity necessary to discriminate local facial features (Canoluk, Moors, & Goffaux, 2023; Goffaux, 2012).

text.text: The results presented here suggest that contextual suppression extends to a more fundamental visual property of the face s mulus, namely local contrast.

In line with past empirical evidence that inversion shrinks the spa al window of face processing (Poltoratski et al., 2021; Rossion, 2008; Van Belle et al., 2010), contextual influence in inverted faces dras cally decreased compared with that observed for upright faces.

text.text: However, context influence was not eliminated by inversion: contrast thresholds were slightly higher when local facial features were presented in context than when they were presented in isola on.
Contextual suppression was stronger for incongruent than congruent context as observed for upright faces.
However, both context types exerted a suppressive influence on local facial feature discrimina on.

This departs from our past findings that context moderately but significantly improved (i.e. lowered) shape dissimilarity threshold for feature discrimina on in inverted faces (Canoluk, Moors, & Goffaux, 2023).

text.text: It is unclear whether this polarity flip of contextual influence across studies for inverted faces might be due to the use of local contrast compared to shape dissimilarity.

The central objec ve of our study was to examine the poten al func onal link between contextual mechanisms at different levels of the visual processing hierarchy and of high-level processing specializa on.

In line with past evidence, we found extreme evidence for the func onal dependence of high-level contextual mechanisms between specialized and non-specialized (upright and inverted, respec vely) face processing (Canoluk, Moors, & Goffaux, 2023).

text.text: The mechanisms shared between upright and inverted face processing accounted for ~30% of the variance in contextual modula on magnitude.

The amount of variance in contextual modula on that remains a er removing this shared variance is further support to the func onal specificity of the contextual mechanisms engaged in the processing of upright faces.

To address func onal rela onship of contextual modula ons across the levels of the visual hierarchy, we systema cally quan fied the shared variance in contextual modula on magnitude between the low-level contrast detec on and the high-level feature discrimina on.

Correla on results did not support the hypothesis of a func onal link between low-level with high-level contextual modula ons, neither for specialized (upright, H1) nor for non-specialized (inverted, H2) face processing.

For upright faces (H1), the data were about three mes more likely under the absence than under the presence of a correla on (BF₀₁ = 3.03), which is moderate evidence for func onal independence, although it falls short of our preregistered eviden al threshold (BF₀₁ > 6).

text.text: Yet, it seems reasonable to defend that V1 encoding determines the percep on of complex natural s muli.

V1 anatomy and connec vity have been shown to determine the perceptual experience of object size and orienta on (Moutsiana et al., 2016; Song et al., 2015; Song et al., 2013 but see Jastrzebowska et al., 2026).

text.text: Moreover, the shared dependence on local input strength indicates similar working principles for contextual modula ons at low-and high-level stages of visual processing.

However, our findings indicate that contextual modula ons in upright faces recruit mechanisms that are func onally similar to but independent from primary contextual mechanisms (Kiniklioglu & Kaiser, 2026; Kiniklioglu, Pitcher, & Kaiser, 2026).

text.text: The fact that the low-level task used here induced near surround contextual modula on may have hindered the emergence of a link with high-level face contextual modula ons.

Indeed, while near (<3° distance) surround suppression results from local lateral interac ons within V1, far surround modula ons (>3° distance) are driven by top-down influences from higher-level brain regions (Bair, Cavanaugh, & Movshon, 2003; Nurminen & Angelucci, 2014; Pokorny, Weldon, & Olman, 2024).

text.text: Using far-surround contextual modula ons may involve system-wide neural communica ons and thus be a more promising avenue to address the link in contextual mechanisms across visual processing levels.
Another aspect that may have hindered the observa on of the func onal link between low-and high-level contextual modula ons is the reliance on purely behavioral measures.

Behavioral responses reflect a long chain of processing, ranging from early sensory encoding to the later stages of decision-making, and may lack the sensi vity and specificity required to highlight varia ons that are selec vely shared by contextual mechanisms.
Indeed, within or between visual domains, contextual modula ons do not or only weakly correlate (Cretenoud, Francis, & Herzog, 2020; Jastrzebowska et al., 2026).

text.text: The different types of decisions involved in low-and high-level tasks (detec on as opposed to discrimina on) may have further obscured the func onal link.
The absence of a reliable correla on between low-and high-level contextual effects may also result from the use of gra ngs in the low-level task.

text.text: To address the func onal link of contextual modula ons across computa onal levels and, more broadly, be er understand how context influences natural vision, it is more promising to use complex natural images and track contextual influences directly on the neural responses at different levels of the visual system hierarchy (for example Goffaux et al., 2016; Kiniklioglu, Pitcher, & Kaiser, 2026; Schuurmans et al., 2023; see Jastrzebowska et al., 2026).

text.text: To conclude, we inves gated whether the behavioral signatures of contextual processing a ributed to low and high levels of the visual system hierarchy are func onally linked at the individual par cipant level.
Despite their sharing of common func onal principles, we found no conclusive evidence for a link between low-and high-level contextual modula ons.

A more promising avenue to progress toward a much-needed system-wide understanding of the influence of spa al context in everyday life vision requires directly inves ga ng contextual influences on the neural representa on of natural images across the levels of the visual system hierarchy.
